summary: Specifies sockets API extensions for the multihoming shim layer, a conceptual sub-layer inside IP on a multihomed host. The API lets applications interact with the shim for locator management and get information about failure detection and path exploration.

eli5.summary: A computer with several network connections has a helper that switches between them. This describes the way programs can talk to that helper, for example to choose a path or learn that one has failed.

questions: how do applications control path selection in multihomed hosts
what are socket options for shim6
how does hip interact with the sockets api
subtitle: API for applications to control multihomed host path selection

tldr.problem: Computers with multiple network connections need a way for applications to control which connection is used, but standard sockets APIs do not provide this control at the identifier-locator level.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines socket options and ancillary data extensions that allow applications to inspect and manipulate the mapping between stable identifiers and the IP addresses (locators) actually used for communication.
tldr.outcome: Applications gain the ability to participate in advanced locator management, failure detection, and path exploration when the OS supports a multihoming shim layer such as Shim6 or HIP.

facts.label: Supported shims
facts.value: Shim6, HIP (one active at a time)

facts.label: Key socket options
facts.value: 15 options for control, locator management, and feedback

today: RFC 6316 is an Informational RFC published in July 2011. Shim6 and HIP have seen limited deployment in production networks, so this API remains primarily a reference for protocol designers and researchers. The specification provides a stable definition for implementations that wish to support multihoming shim layers, but wide adoption would require significant OS-level infrastructure changes to support the shim sub-layer itself.

sections.title: Multihoming and the Shim Concept
sections.content:
A multihomed host has multiple network connections. This could be a laptop with both WiFi and Ethernet, a phone with both cellular and WiFi, or a server with multiple network cards. The problem is that Internet addresses serve two purposes: they identify who you are talking to (the identifier), and they specify the current path to reach you (the locator). When a host moves between networks or a path fails, the locator changes but the identifier should remain stable.

The RFC assumes a conceptual shim sub-layer inside the IP layer that maintains mappings between stable identifiers and changing locators. This shim could be a protocol like Shim6 (a standardized multihoming protocol) or HIP (Host Identity Protocol). The shim layer intercepts IP packets, rewrites their source and destination addresses to reflect current working locators, and maintains the mapping so upper-layer protocols do not notice the changes.

The challenge this RFC addresses is how applications and upper-layer protocols can interact with this shim layer. Without an API, applications are blind to what the shim is doing and cannot provide hints about what works or failed.
sections.eli5: A helper inside the IP layer switches between paths as needed. Programs need a way to tell this helper what they prefer, and ask which path is being used.

sections.title: Identifiers, Locators, and Contexts
sections.content:
The RFC defines several key terms. An Endpoint Identifier (EID) is the stable address programs use (like a home address or public key hash). A Locator is the actual IP address on the wire. A Context is the state information for a pair of peers, storing which locators are associated with each EID. A ULID (Upper-Layer Identifier, used in Shim6) is an identifier chosen from available locators. A Host Identifier (in HIP) is cryptographically derived.

Applications use the traditional sockets API with EIDs as addresses. The shim layer below transparently maintains lists of working and preferred locators for each direction (local and peer). When a path fails, the shim's REAP module (Reachability Protocol) detects the outage and explores alternate locator pairs. Applications can request hot-standby mode, where the shim pre-validates alternative paths so switches are immediate, or ask the shim to provide feedback about which locators were actually used.
sections.eli5: Programs see a stable name. Below, a helper layer tracks many possible paths to reach that name and switches automatically when needed. Programs can watch and guide this process.

sections.title: Socket Options and Ancillary Data
sections.content:
The API extends sockets with new socket options at a dedicated level, SOL_SHIM. Critical options include:

Control options: SHIM_DONTSHIM tells the shim not to apply multihoming to this socket (useful to avoid conflict with SCTP or multipath TCP). SHIM_HOT_STANDBY requests the shim to maintain hot-standby (pre-validated alternative paths). SHIM_ASSOCIATED is read-only and tells whether the socket has an active shim context.

Locator management: SHIM_LOC_LOCAL_PREF and SHIM_LOC_PEER_PREF set preferred source and destination locators. SHIM_LOCLIST_LOCAL and SHIM_LOCLIST_PEER get or set the full list of available locators. SHIM_LOC_LOCAL_SEND and SHIM_LOC_PEER_SEND allow setting or querying the specific locators used for outgoing traffic.

Feedback: SHIM_APP_TIMEOUT lets applications set how long the shim should wait before deciding a path has failed. SHIM_PATHEXPLORE controls how aggressively the shim explores alternatives. Ancillary data (cmsg) allows querying which locator pair was actually used for a received packet.
sections.eli5: New socket options let programs turn the shim on or off, choose preferred paths, and get a list of available paths. Special data in received packets tells the program which path that data took.

sections.title: System Requirements and Compatibility
sections.content:
The API is designed to coexist with existing sockets APIs. Legacy applications see only the identifier (EID) and do not need changes. New applications can use the shim options to gain control. The system model places the shim as a separate layer independent of address family (IPv4/IPv6) and transport protocol (TCP/UDP), allowing the same options to work across combinations.

The RFC addresses the challenge that only one shim can be active at a time (Shim6 or HIP, but not both simultaneously) to avoid conflicts. Applications can query whether deferred context setup is supported, allowing them to work with both Shim6 (which defers context setup until communication starts, useful if the ULID is routable) and HIP (which requires establishing context before communication).

Error handling is defined for common cases: EOPNOTSUPP when an operation is not supported, ENOENT when requested without a context, EINVALIDLOCATOR when a locator is invalid. Security considerations include validating unknown locators and treating source/destination locators separately to prevent spoofing.
sections.eli5: Old programs work as before. New programs can ask for extra control. Only one multihoming system can run, to avoid confusion. The API warns when something is not available or invalid.

sections.title: Applications and Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC is aimed at application developers who would benefit from explicit locator control. Examples include voice-over-IP applications sensitive to latency, which might request hot-standby to minimize handover delay, or video streaming applications that can tolerate slower failover but want to know which path is active for QoS monitoring.

Upper-layer protocols like TCP can provide feedback to the shim. A TCP stack detecting retransmissions and timeouts can signal this to REAP, triggering path exploration. Applications can suppress keepalives on paths they know are idle. The API supports context forking (as documented in the appendix), allowing a single socket to branch into multiple contexts when a host with multiple locators connects to a multihomed peer.

The document notes practical deployment scenarios where IPv4 and IPv6 locators coexist, and NAT handling for locators (HIP supports private IPv4 addresses as locators when behind NAT, whereas Shim6 works only with IPv6).
sections.eli5: Voice calls can ask for instant failover. Video streams can ask to be told which path they are using. The helper tells the program when a path is broken so it can take action.
